statement: In 24 healthy adults with previous LSD experience given a single low laboratory dose of LSD and, on another day, a placebo (one randomized, double-blind crossover study in Brazil; Wiessner et al., 2022), the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD changes thinking the next morning. In models adjusted for body mass index and time since last psychedelic use, people recalled a complex drawing and card locations somewhat better and named more words beginning with a given letter after LSD than after placebo, but did worse on a card-sorting test of mental flexibility (fewer categories completed, more errors and repeated wrong answers), with partial eta squared from 0.19 to 0.34; attention, self-control, reasoning, word-list memory and drawing fluency did not differ. About 66 test scores were analysed without correction for multiple testing, the authors report that the unadjusted analyses showed few differences, practice effects were large, the paper's text and table disagree on the direction of two card-sorting scores, and a few people account for much of the card-sorting difference in the figure. The study did not measure mood or sleep. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Twenty-four people who had taken LSD before took a small dose in a lab, and a dummy drink on another day. The next morning they did memory, word and puzzle tests. After LSD, a few memory and word scores were a little better and one card-sorting puzzle was a little worse than after the dummy drink. These small differences may be chance, because many scores were checked. Mood and sleep were not measured.
population: Healthy adults aged 25 to 61 (8 of 24 women) with at least one previous LSD experience and no psychiatric illness, in a laboratory study in Campinas, Brazil
exposure: A single low oral dose of LSD given by researchers in the morning (amount and timing are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people after an inactive placebo in a separate session two weeks apart
outcome: Performance on memory, fluency, mental flexibility, attention, inhibition and reasoning tests the next morning
magnitude: Adjusted models, LSD against placebo: drawing recall F(1,20) = 4.63, p = 0.044, partial eta squared 0.19 (points) and 6.62, p = 0.018, 0.25 (percentage); card-location consolidation F(1,19) = 6.23, p = 0.022, 0.25; letter fluency F(1,20) = 5.08, p = 0.036, 0.20; card sorting, categories achieved F(1,20) = 8.11, p = 0.010, 0.29 (fewer), total errors 7.86, p = 0.011, 0.28, perseverative errors type 3 9.55, p = 0.006, 0.32. No means or confidence intervals in the main text.

evidence.locator: Methods 2.6 Data analysis (p. 10); Table 1, Period effects (p. 11); Discussion 4.4 Limitations (p. 15)
evidence.extracted: Exploratory analysis without correction for multiple comparisons; covariates added after the unadjusted models; the authors state that the analyses without covariates yielded few treatment effects and many period effects. Practice (period) effects were significant for drawing recall, letter fluency, design fluency (F(1,20) = 20.0, p<0.001, 0.50), Trail Making and Stroop.

evidence.locator: Table 1, WCST CL (%) and NE (%) rows (p. 11); Fig. 1 D (p. 12); Results 3.3 (p. 13)
evidence.extracted: The text says LSD decreased the percentage of conceptual level responses and increased the percentage of non-perseverative errors, while Table 1 and Fig. 1 show the reverse for both (CL (%) higher after LSD, F(1,20) = 6.78, p = 0.017; NE (%) lower, F(1,20) = 5.36, p = 0.031). Fig. 1 shows single-subject lines in which a few participants had much larger card-sorting error counts after LSD (editors' visual reading, values not extracted).

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 high for selection of the reported result: no registration, about 66 variables without correction, effects shown from covariate-adjusted models after the unadjusted models showed few; blinding not checked.

indirectness.note: Worded for one low laboratory dose in experienced healthy volunteers.

imprecision.note: 24 people; no confidence intervals or means in the main text.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled crossover with randomized order starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -2 (reported results depend on an analysis choice among many uncorrected tests) and imprecision -1 give very low. Insufficient evidence: the significant differences are small, run in both directions, and may not survive correction or the unadjusted analysis, while the null tests are too imprecise to show no effect.
